newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court deals setback to term-limit measure.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court deals setback to term-limit measure.

text.p: The Supreme Court Monday let stand a ruling striking down a voter initiative instructing state and federal lawmakers to use the power of their offices to pass a constitutional term-limit amendment for Congress.
The high court denied appeals in an Arkansas case defending the so-called "instruct and inform" state initiatives on term limits and asking the justices to declare them constitutional.
The Supreme Court's action, in a one-line order, dealt another setback to supporters of a constitutional term-limit amendment, a proposal that recently was rejected in the Congress.

Under the proposed constitutional amendment at issue in the case, U.S. senators would be limited to two six-year terms while members of the U.S. House of Representatives could serve three two-year terms.

The Arkansas measure also provided that lawmakers who ignored it will have the following note printed by their names on the ballot for the next election, "Disregarded voter instructions on term limits."
The Supreme Court last dealt with term limits in May 1995 when it ruled by a 5-4 vote that states on their own cannot limit the length of time members of Congress may serve.

But supporters of term limits, which are seen as a way of making Congress more responsive to the people by getting rid of entrenched lawmakers, then turned their efforts toward passing a constitutional amendment.

The Arkansas initiative was approved in the November election by a vote of 61 to 39 percent. Virtually identical measures also were adopted in Alaska, Colorado, Idaho, Maine, Missouri, Nebraska, Nevada and South Dakota.

The new initiatives were aimed at getting the required two-thirds vote in Congress so the constitutional amendment could be taken up by the states. Approval then would be needed in three fourths of the state legislatures or in a convention called by two thirds of the state legislatures.

Although the Republican "Contract with America" called for term limits, the constitutional amendment has failed to get the necessary votes in Congress. The House on Feb. 12 defeated the proposal, and it received fewer votes than in 1995.
The Arkansas Supreme Court declared that the state initiative unconstitutionally sought to give legislative powers directly to the people and was "coercive" of the legislators.
It also ruled that the measure violated the federal constitutional dictate that all amendments to the U.S. Constitution originate in Congress or state legislatures.

The justices, without comment or dissent, left intact the state court ruling. The high court's action does not create national precedent and does not have the force of a ruling, but it can be cited in other cases.

Arkansas and a group advocating term limits appealed to the Supreme Court in defending the measure and asking the justices to hear the case. Supporting them were Nebraska, Colorado, South Carolina and South Dakota.

Paul Jacobs, executive director of the group U.S. Term Limits, criticised the state court decision. "Nobody in Congress is required to do as the people have asked in this initiative. The law merely stipulates that the voters be informed."

Opponents said the measure unfairly threatens legislators and added that a lawmaker may be obeying the wishes of voters in that district by opposing term limits. Also, a lawmaker may support a different term limit proposal, they said.
